By Thomas Novelly · Nov 19, 2026

Good morning, y'all! Welcome back to our space edition.

It's Future of Defense Summit day. Can't wait to see y'all there! If you can't make it, you can watch the livestream here.

🍗 Programming note: Colin Demarest and I will bring you a joint newsletter on Tuesday. There will be no space edition on Thanksgiving.

  • Enjoy the food and your loved ones! We're grateful to have you as readers.

🚀 Watch this space: Let's look at the U.S. launch crunch, "Google Maps" for space, Toyota's space drive and a bit more.

Today's newsletter is 1,754 words, a 6.5-minute read.
 
 
1 big thing: America's "launch crisis"
 

Illustration: Aïda Amer/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
 

While SpaceX basked in its historic Starship "catch" last weekend, a different space mission went awry the next day — with serious implications for U.S. national security.

  • United Launch Alliance's heavy-lift Vulcan rocket had a mission failure Sunday just 10 minutes into its mission to bring 40 Amazon Leo satellites to space.

Why it matters: The growing commercial space industry and future U.S. military missions depend on multiple reliable rocket providers.

  • But only two companies have flown National Security Space Launch missions: ULA and SpaceX. The former just had a mission failure, and the latter may be winding down government launches.
  • Blue Origin will eventually become a third provider once its New Glenn rocket, which exploded on the launchpad in May, meets the required number of certification flights. The company is targeting January to return to flight, according to an internal memo.
  • "It is very concerning, especially when the three main Pentagon providers are SpaceX, ULA and Blue Origin," Emmerson Overell, a research analyst at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told me. "And Blue Origin's New Glenn heavy rocket has also been grounded."

What they're saying: ULA said in a press statement that it's investigating the cause and "[w]e truly understand the impact this has on our customers."

  • ULA said yesterday that "preliminary indications" are that Vulcan's low booster thrust was the result of inadequate fuel supply and not an issue with the engines itself.
  • The jointly owned Boeing and Lockheed Martin business had to sideline Vulcan in February for national security missions as it investigated a booster problem.

Threat level: SpaceX's Starship development and ULA's mission failure have wide-ranging repercussions for national security and the satellite business.

  • SpaceX plans to scale down the use of the reusable, medium-lift Falcon 9 rocket that's been the workhorse of the space industry and the U.S. military's operations.
  • The company is going all in on its super-heavy-lift Starship — which was seemingly built with Starlink satellites, not other military or commercial payloads, in mind.
  • ULA's Vulcan failure hurts not only Space Force but also Amazon, which partially relies on the rockets to launch satellites for its emerging space-based internet service.
  • "Even once they get back to flight, how long is it going to take for them to get certified again to launch these sensitive national security payloads?" Todd Harrison, the American Enterprise Institute's space expert, told me. "This is a real mess."
  • Brig. Gen. Eric Zarybnisky, the Space Force officer who oversees national security launches, said in a statement that rocket innovation is "inherently challenging" and that the military will support ULA "in a rigorous, data-driven analysis" of Sunday's incident.
  • The Space Force said in a statement it "secures a variety of providers to ensure no single vehicle transition impacts national security" and expressed confidence that its providers will be able to launch national security missions "in the coming months."

By the numbers: Prior to ULA's mishap, Quilty Space, a market research firm, projected a shortfall of around 150 medium- and heavy-lift rocket launches through 2030, according to a report shared with Axios.

  • There are 44 medium- and heavy-lift missions facing capacity constraints in 2028, making it the "most acute year of the launch crisis," the report said.

Case in point: Commercial satellite companies and startups are now booking rockets that haven't flown yet; others want to build their own.

Reality check: Established rocket makers "typically missed their inaugural launch targets by two to four years," according to Quilty's report.

  • New providers average fewer than three launches annually during their first five years, it said.

The bottom line: Caleb Henry, Quilty's research director, told me "every failure makes the launch shortage worse," as more critical missions pile up.
 
 
2. Exclusive: HEO's space map
 

HEO's new Insights Next platform aims to be the "Google Maps" of outer space intelligence. Photo: Courtesy of HEO
 

HEO, an Australian company, has been taking thousands of images of objects in orbit and has woven them together in a new space intelligence platform, Axios has learned.

Why it matters: As space warfare looms, countries need to be able to track potentially hostile activities in orbit to protect their military and commercial satellites from interference or attack.

  • In October, an orbital showdown between a Russian spacecraft and a U.S. ICEYE satellite illustrated why keeping a close eye on space is crucial for emerging conflicts.

What he's saying: HEO's CEO William Crowe told me the firm has sensors and software that can be used with maneuverable imaging satellites to capture detailed photos of spacecraft, akin to orbital paparazzi.

  • "We've got sensors in all different orbits that can look at objects at different angles," Crowe said. "Now, there's really nowhere to hide."
  • Crowe said HEO's customers wanted to gather even more intelligence and information from those images, which led to the creation of the firm's new Insights Next platform.

How it works: Think of it like "Google Maps" for space. Using information from 7,500 imaging missions across 1,200 unique objects, HEO has put all the data into its Insights Next platform.

  • Users can see what was once a 2D image of a satellite as a 3D model.
  • It also shows a satellite's "position relative to Earth, orientation, dimensions, payload configuration and pointing direction," according to HEO.
  • HEO said the platform allows total inspection of a satellite to see how it operates, what its purpose might be and whether its orbit or behavior changes.

Follow the money: HEO is growing.

  • In September, the Australian space firm raised $25 million in Series B funding to expand its imaging capabilities from low-Earth orbit to a much larger geostationary orbit.
  • HEO's imaging has also supported a wide range of U.S. and allied militaries, including the U.S. National Reconnaissance Office, the Australian Department of Defence, Japan's Ministry of Defense and the U.K. Space Agency, the firm said.

The bottom line: Crowe told me that the ability to closely monitor space activity will reveal the rapid pace of military space developments.

  • "The craziest is definitely still yet to come," Crowe said.
 
 
3. Toyota's space drive
By Joann Muller and Thomas Novelly
 

Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
 

Toyota, the Japanese industrial giant that evolved from making textile looms to building cars, is exploring another potentially transformative business opportunity: space.

Why it matters: The booming space industry has a manufacturing problem — and Toyota thinks it can help solve it.

  • As demand for satellites soars, Toyota sees an opportunity to apply its expertise in efficient, high-volume manufacturing to an industry that has traditionally relied on expensive, custom-built spacecraft.

Driving the news: Toyota revealed its space ambitions in an exclusive interview with Axios, disclosing for the first time that it has invested more than $240 million in 11 space-related startups.

  • The investments, through Toyota's three investment arms — Toyota Ventures, Woven Capital and Toyota Invention Partners — span satellite manufacturing, communications, navigation, rocket launches and spacecraft servicing.

Between the lines: Toyota's space investments could benefit both its automotive business and the emerging space industry.

  • For Toyota, they could mean better satellite connectivity, more precise navigation and new revenue streams beyond automobiles.
  • For space companies, Toyota brings established supply chains and manufacturing expertise that could help them overcome production bottlenecks and lower costs.

The space companies Toyota is investing in are:

  • Stoke Space
  • CesiumAstro
  • Interstellar
  • Apex Space
  • Xona Space
  • Muon Space
  • Starfish Space
  • Rendezvous Robotics
  • Matter Intelligence
  • Warpspace
  • Cosmobloom

4. ICYMI: Space data center risks
 

Illustration: Brendan Lynch/Axios
 

Sprawling networks of space data centers could make it nearly impossible for humans to stargaze.

  • That's just one of the many risks that come with placing tens of thousands of AI computers into orbit, according to a new report.

Why it matters: Most Americans don't want data centers built near them, but putting them in space brings a new set of problems.

Threat level: "Companies and policymakers should proceed with great caution," top academic researchers warn in a report for the Innovation for Cool Earth Forum, an annual event hosted by the Japanese government.

  • If space data centers proliferate, the "most visible points of light in the sky during much of the night in much of the world could be satellites, not stars," the report said, mirroring astronomers' worries.
  • If the U.S. military adopts the technology, the data centers could become potential targets during future space conflicts.
  • Thousands of orbital data centers whipping around the Earth at 17,000 miles per hour mean a growing "risk of collisions" and dangerous space debris.

Read more here.
 
 
5. Quick hits
 

Illustration: Shoshana Gordon/Axios
 

🎓 Multiple states are making bids to host the U.S. Space Academy.

  • The big picture: Axios reporters John Frank and Ryan Deto covered pitches from Colorado Springs and Pittsburgh, respectively. Maryland and Virginia are also making moves, Axios' Mimi Montgomery reports.
  • 💭 My thought bubble: It seems like nearly every state is making a pitch for Trump's Space Academy, but the question is whether the new Congress will ultimately provide funding.

📡 RBC Signals netted a $10 million strategic growth investment from Washington Harbour Partners, the firm announced today.

  • Why it matters: Washington Harbour Partners has a wide range of space investments, from SpaceX to startups, and now it's eyeing the Redmond, Washington, data and satellite connectivity firm's tech.
  • 💭 My thought bubble: I'll be chatting with Washington Harbour Partners CEO and founder Mina Faltas at the Axios Future of Defense Summit today to unpack this investment.

💥 Ursa Major and Avio USA netted a joint RTX contract to develop solid-rocket motors for the Tomahawk cruise missile, my colleague Colin reports.

  • Why it matters: The work is expected to produce a pair of qualified booster vendors to support one of the most in-demand munitions in the U.S. inventory.
  • 💭 Colin's thought bubble: "Few people have wielded the Tomahawk cruise missile like Commander in Chief Donald Trump. More Tomahawk contributors is a good thing for the U.S. and potential buyers."
 
 
6. Check this out
 

HEO imagery of Russian satellite Kondor-FKA 2. Photo: Courtesy of HEO
 

🛰️ HEO captured an image of a newer Russian spacecraft with one of the satellites in its network

Why it matters: It's a snapshot showing Russia's space advancements.

  • The image, shared with Axios, shows Kondor-FKA 2, an Earth-observation satellite that was launched in November 2024.
 
 

A MESSAGE FROM JPMORGANCHASE

The U.S. defense industrial base faces a production gap
 
 

A JPMorganChase Center for Geopolitics report finds that U.S. defense innovation is accelerating, but production capacity is struggling to keep pace.

Outdated procurement processes and limited industrial capacity make it difficult to turn emerging technology into production at scale.
